title: 10 — Entity Resolution, Ontology and Relationship Graphs
html:
10 — Entity Resolution, Ontology and Relationship Graphs

The one idea: before numbers from different sources can be compared, every record must point at the same real-world entity. Match on identifiers first, fall back to probabilistic matching of names and attributes, send the uncertain middle to a person — then describe entities with a shared vocabulary (an ontology) and connect them in a graph to see groups and contagion paths.

1. Entity resolution — definition

Entity resolution (ER) — also called record linkage or de-duplication — decides which records refer to the same real-world thing, and assigns each cluster a canonical ID.

Inputs look like this:

Source Name Identifier City
Exchange filing Example Steel Limited CIN L27100MH1990PLC012345 Mumbai
Rating report EXAMPLE STEEL LTD. — Mumbai
Lender file Example Steel Ltd PAN AAACE1234F Mumbai
News Example Steel — —

All four are one entity. A naive join on name finds none of them equal.

2. The three-tier approach

---
title: Three-tier entity resolution
---
flowchart TD
    R["Incoming records"] --> N["Normalise names and identifiers"]
    N --> T1{"Tier 1: exact identifier match<br/>(LEI, CIN, PAN, ISIN to issuer)"}
    T1 -->|match| C["Assign canonical ID"]
    T1 -->|no identifier| T2["Tier 2: probabilistic matching<br/>(Splink / RapidFuzz)"]
    T2 -->|"probability >= 0.95"| C
    T2 -->|"0.70 to 0.95"| T3["Tier 3: human steward review"]
    T2 -->|"< 0.70"| NEW["Create new entity"]
    T3 -->|confirmed| C
    T3 -->|rejected| NEW

2.1 Normalisation (always first)

import re, unicodedata

SUFFIXES = r"\b(limited|ltd|private|pvt|plc|llp|inc|corp|corporation|company|co)\b\.?"

def normalise_name(s: str) -> str:
    s = unicodedata.normalize("NFKC", s).lower()
    s = s.replace("&", " and ")
    s = re.sub(r"[^\w\s]", " ", s)
    s = re.sub(SUFFIXES, " ", s)
    return re.sub(r"\s+", " ", s).strip()

normalise_name("EXAMPLE STEEL LTD.")   # 'example steel'

Normalise identifiers too: upper-case, strip spaces, validate check digits (chapter 01).

2.2 Tier 1 — deterministic

If two records share a valid LEI, CIN or PAN, they are the same entity. An ISIN maps to its issuer (via an instrument master), not to an entity directly. Keep an entity_identifier table: (canonical_id, id_type, id_value, valid_from, valid_to, source).

2.3 Tier 2 — probabilistic with Fellegi–Sunter

For each candidate pair, compare fields and compute how much each comparison outcome shifts the odds of a match:

  • m-probability = P(fields agree | records are a match)
  • u-probability = P(fields agree | records are not a match)
  • Match weight = log₂(m / u). Agreement on a rare surname or exact PAN adds a lot; agreement on city adds little; disagreement subtracts.
  • Sum the weights (plus a prior), convert to a probability.

Comparing every pair is O(n²), so blocking rules restrict comparisons to pairs that share something cheap (same state, same first 3 letters of normalised name, same postcode).

2.4 Splink in practice (DuckDB backend)

import splink.comparison_library as cl
from splink import DuckDBAPI, Linker, SettingsCreator, block_on

settings = SettingsCreator(
    link_type="dedupe_only",
    unique_id_column_name="record_id",
    blocking_rules_to_generate_predictions=[
        block_on("name_prefix"),           # first 4 chars of normalised name
        block_on("state"),
    ],
    comparisons=[
        cl.JaroWinklerAtThresholds("name_norm", [0.95, 0.88]),
        cl.ExactMatch("pan"),
        cl.ExactMatch("city").configure(term_frequency_adjustments=True),
        cl.LevenshteinAtThresholds("registered_address", [2, 5]),
    ],
)

linker = Linker(records_df, settings, db_api=DuckDBAPI())

# Learn parameters: u from random pairs, m by expectation-maximisation
linker.training.estimate_u_using_random_sampling(max_pairs=1e6)
linker.training.estimate_parameters_using_expectation_maximisation(block_on("pan"))
linker.training.estimate_parameters_using_expectation_maximisation(block_on("name_prefix"))

pairs = linker.inference.predict(threshold_match_probability=0.70)
clusters = linker.clustering.cluster_pairwise_predictions_at_threshold(pairs, threshold_match_probability=0.95)

linker.visualisations.match_weights_chart()           # inspect what drives decisions

2.5 RapidFuzz for quick lookups

When you need "best match for this one name against a master list" rather than full de-duplication:

from rapidfuzz import fuzz, process, utils

master = ["example steel", "example motors", "national steel works"]     # already normalised
process.extractOne(normalise_name("EXAMPLE STEEL LTD."), master, scorer=fuzz.token_sort_ratio,
                   processor=utils.default_process)
# ('example steel', 100.0, 0) — a name score alone is never enough; combine with other evidence

fuzz.WRatio("Larsen & Toubro", "Larsen and Toubro Limited")   # robust mixed scorer

2.6 Tier 3 — steward review

Pairs in the uncertain band go to a queue with evidence side by side: both records, the source documents with highlighted bounding boxes (chapter 11), and the match-weight breakdown. Steward decisions are stored and fed back as training labels.

2.7 Measuring ER

Build a labelled sample. Report precision (of pairs we merged, how many were right) and recall (of true pairs, how many we found). In finance, a false merge (two different borrowers become one) is usually worse than a missed merge — tune thresholds for precision.

3. Triangulation and survivorship

When three sources give three different values for the same fact, decide which one "survives" into Silver/Gold.

Corroboration score per candidate value: how many independent sources agree (within tolerance), weighted by source reliability.

import polars as pl

candidates = pl.DataFrame({
    "entity_id": ["E1"] * 3,
    "metric": ["total_debt"] * 3,
    "source": ["annual_report", "rating_report", "data_vendor"],
    "value": [5200.0, 5200.0, 5350.0],
    "source_rank": [1, 2, 3],                  # from a versioned survivorship rule
    "published_at": ["2026-05-18", "2026-06-01", "2026-05-20"],
})

tol = 0.005   # 0.5%
scored = (
    candidates.join(candidates.select("entity_id", "metric", pl.col("value").alias("other")),
                    on=["entity_id", "metric"])
    .with_columns(agrees=((pl.col("value") - pl.col("other")).abs() / pl.col("value") <= tol))
    .group_by("entity_id", "metric", "source", "value", "source_rank", "published_at")
    .agg(corroboration=pl.col("agrees").sum())          # includes itself
    .sort(["corroboration", "source_rank"], descending=[True, False])
)
survivor = scored.group_by("entity_id", "metric").first()

Survivorship rules — examples, stored as versioned data with approvers:

  1. Prefer the value corroborated by the most independent sources.
  2. Tie → prefer the primary source (the issuer's own filing) over secondary.
  3. Tie → prefer the most recently published.
  4. If the best corroboration is 1 and sources differ by more than tolerance → do not choose; raise an exception for review.

Corporate actions (splits, bonuses, mergers, name changes) must be applied before comparing per-share figures or names across time.

4. Ontology: FIBO

4.1 Taxonomy vs ontology

  • Taxonomy: a hierarchy of categories (Security → Equity → Common share).
  • Ontology: classes plus properties and relationships with formal meaning (a DebtInstrument hasIssuer a LegalEntity; a CreditRating isAssignedBy a RatingAgency and rates an instrument or entity).

4.2 FIBO

The Financial Industry Business Ontology, maintained by the EDM Council, is an open OWL ontology covering financial concepts. Main domains:

Domain Covers
FND — Foundations Agents, dates, quantities, ownership, control
BE — Business Entities Legal entities, corporations, ownership and control relationships
FBC — Financial Business & Commerce Financial services, registration authorities, regulators, products
SEC — Securities Equities, debt, funds, identifiers
DER — Derivatives Options, swaps, futures
LOAN Loan products and contracts
IND — Indicators Rates, indices, economic indicators
CAE — Corporate Actions & Events Splits, dividends, mergers

4.3 How to use it practically

You rarely run a full OWL reasoner in a data pipeline. Instead:

  1. Map each extracted field and table to a FIBO class or property URI — store it in a mapping table or in the data contract (businessName, authoritativeDefinitions).
  2. Extend with local concepts FIBO lacks (Indian identifiers like CIN and PAN, SEBI scheme categories, RBI asset classification) in your own namespace, linked to the nearest FIBO class.
  3. Use the mapping to drive consistent naming across tables, to build a glossary, and to give AI agents precise definitions.
# mapping example
- field: silver.financial_fact.entity_id
  concept: fibo-be: LegalEntity          # look up the exact IRI in the FIBO viewer
- field: silver.instrument.isin
  concept: fibo-sec: InternationalSecuritiesIdentificationNumber
- field: silver.rating.rating_symbol
  concept: fibo-fbc: CreditRating
- field: silver.entity_identifier[id_type='CIN']
  concept: local: CorporateIdentificationNumber   # local extension, subclass of a FIBO identifier class

5. Relationship graphs and contagion

5.1 Why a graph

Credit risk travels through relationships: a promoter pledges shares across group companies, a shared auditor resigns from several, a lender is exposed to an entire group. Tables answer "what is this entity's debt?"; graphs answer "who else is affected if it defaults?"

---
title: Issuer relationship graph
---
flowchart LR
    G["Group holding"] -->|owns 60%| A["Issuer A"]
    G -->|owns 45%| B["Issuer B"]
    P["Promoter"] -->|controls| G
    P -->|"pledged shares"| A
    D["Director X"] -->|board seat| A
    D -->|board seat| C["Issuer C"]
    AU["Auditor Y"] -->|audits| A
    AU -->|audits| B
    L["Lender Z"] -->|lends to| A
    L -->|lends to| C

5.2 Build and analyse with NetworkX

import networkx as nx

g = nx.DiGraph()
g.add_edge("group_holding", "issuer_a", rel="owns", pct=0.60)
g.add_edge("group_holding", "issuer_b", rel="owns", pct=0.45)
g.add_edge("promoter", "group_holding", rel="controls")
g.add_edge("lender_z", "issuer_a", rel="lends", amount=1200)
g.add_edge("lender_z", "issuer_c", rel="lends", amount=800)
g.add_edge("auditor_y", "issuer_a", rel="audits")
g.add_edge("auditor_y", "issuer_b", rel="audits")

# Everything reachable from the promoter: the controlled group
nx.descendants(g, "promoter")                      # {'group_holding', 'issuer_a', 'issuer_b'}

# Who is connected to issuer_a in any direction, within 2 hops
nx.ego_graph(g.to_undirected(), "issuer_a", radius=2).nodes

# Central nodes: concentration risk
nx.betweenness_centrality(g.to_undirected())
nx.pagerank(g)

# Contagion path between two issuers, e.g. issuer_b -> auditor_y -> issuer_a -> lender_z -> issuer_c
nx.shortest_path(g.to_undirected(), "issuer_b", "issuer_c")

Use Neo4j (Cypher) when the graph is large, shared by many users, or queried interactively; NetworkX is ideal for analysis in a pipeline. Store edges as a bitemporal Silver table (from_id, to_id, rel, attributes, valid_from, valid_to, known_from) and build the graph for any date.

6. Questions to test yourself

  1. Why does ISIN not resolve an entity directly?
  2. Explain m- and u-probabilities, and why agreement on a common city name adds little weight.
  3. What do blocking rules trade off?
  4. Write three survivorship rules and the case where none should pick a winner.
  5. Taxonomy vs ontology — give one relationship FIBO expresses that a taxonomy cannot.
  6. Which graph measure identifies a lender most exposed to one promoter group?

7. Review checklist

  • Names and identifiers normalised before matching.
  • Deterministic tier runs first; probabilistic thresholds tuned for precision.
  • Uncertain pairs go to a steward queue with evidence; decisions stored.
  • Survivorship rules are versioned data with approvers.
  • Every Silver column mapped to a FIBO (or local extension) concept.
  • Relationship edges stored bitemporally; graph rebuilt per as-of date.
